An automated system scans feedback to detect failures, distinguishing between product-wide improvements and misconfigurations. This creates a closed-loop feedback flywheel.

what_they_built: Three-step mental model to identify and prioritize AI integration points across the SDLC

summary: The team at the Bank of New York developed a three-step mental model to identify and prioritize where AI should be embedded across the software development lifecycle. The goal was to de-risk the organization from an AI surge by focusing on where systems would fail under higher velocity, and to guide targeted automation and infrastructure improvements.

what_they_built: Enforcement policy that only one event type can be emitted to a single Kafka topic
summary: CloudFlare implemented a policy that only one type of event can be emitted to a single Kafka topic—e.g., only 'user-created' events to the 'User Created Event' topic. This rule is enforced via automated checks in the development workflow. If a developer tries to send a different event type (e.g., 'account-created') to that topic, the system rejects the change. This prevents accidental mixing of event types, which could cause downstream systems to fail or misbehave. The policy is part of a broader effort to manage Kafka as a reliable, long-term data source, not just a message bus. It helps ensure that event structure changes are intentional and visible across the organization.
why: To prevent accidental mixing of event types in a topic, which could cause chaos in downstream systems, especially in a system where data is append-only and history cannot be rewritten
how_it_works: The team enforces a rule that only one type of event (e.g., 'user-created') can be emitted to a single topic (e.g., 'User Created Event'). This is enforced via automated checks in the CI/CD pipeline. If a developer tries to send a different event type to that topic, the system rejects the change. This policy is applied across all Kafka topics and is tied to versioned event types (e.g., v1, v2).
outcome: The team made a slightly controversial decision that has been a good one for Kafka adoption
outcome_later: The team has not had any real issues with schema or changes to messages since implementing the enforcement policy.
quote: The slightly controversial decision we made, that I think has been a good one for Kafka adoption, is we made it so you can only emit one event type to one topic. You could have a user-created event, you could have account-created event, you could have account [unintelligible] they could all go to the same topic, and a service may read all of them and care about all of them. A key example was inviting a minoritized team member to silently shadow her at a critical decision-making meeting, which opened doors for them. The framework emphasizes that sponsorship is not just vouching, but providing the actual support needed to succeed—such as access to influential spaces—rather than assuming more advice is required.

how_it_works: The framework involves sponsors actively advocating for and supporting minoritized talent to gain visibility and access to high-impact opportunities, such as being invited to shadow at key decision-making meetings. Sponsors are encouraged to co-create support plans, including check-ins and resources, to reduce risk and increase success.
quote: Members of minoritized communities are over-mentored but under-sponsored. It's particularly valuable during uncertain or failing phases, like the 'falling' part of the J-curve, where learning is most critical. The practice helps people realize that many questions they think are dumb are actually shared by others, and that asking them builds trust and clarity.

It's framed as a deliberate strategy to gain clarity, surface hidden assumptions, and foster psychological safety.

summary: The artifact is a 10-minute interactive session used in training to teach people how language models work. It begins with a prompt: 'Peanut butter and?' where participants instinctively say 'jelly'. The facilitator uses this to demonstrate tokenization, showing how 'peanut butter' breaks into tokens (e.g., 'peanut', 'butter') and how the model predicts the next token based on numerical patterns. Then, by introducing new context like 'Elvis' or 'Graceland', the model's output shifts to 'banana', showing how context alters probability. The session continues by visualizing the context window with hash marks, demonstrating that when it fills up, earlier tokens are discarded. This helps users understand that the model doesn't 'remember' everything and that it's not a perfect memory, but a pattern-matching system. The goal is to build good AI usage habits by giving users awareness of how the model works and what can go wrong.
why: to help people understand how language models work at a fundamental level so they can use them effectively and avoid common pitfalls

The facilitator uses the model's output (jelly) to demonstrate tokenization, showing how words are broken into tokens and represented as numbers. Then, by introducing new context (e.g., 'Elvis', 'Graceland'), the model's output shifts to 'banana', illustrating how context alters token probabilities. The facilitator then uses a visual board to show token stacking and context window limits, demonstrating how older content gets dropped when the limit is reached. This builds awareness of context scarcity and the model's limitations, helping users develop good AI usage habits.

The portal uses a plugin model so that teams like security or infrastructure can contribute code back to the platform. This enables an inner-sourcing model where expertise is distributed across teams, and the central team only maintains the core. The goal is to drive long-term improvement in developer experience, not just check a technology box.
why: to drive a journey around improving developer experience as a whole and being able to really, truly make an impact there
how_it_works: The internal developer portal is built on Backstage and managed by a central team of about six people. Other teams contribute back via a plugin model—e.g., security teams can provide code to implement features in the portal. This supports an inner-sourcing model where expertise is pushed to the edge, and the central team maintains the core platform while enabling decentralized contributions.
quote: I look at that as kind of a bottom-up approach. It's very easy to go out and grab something like Backstage, be able to get it up and running in a few days and be able to show some value there. Well, that becomes harder and harder to do as you're trying to implement things across your organization and being able to change process, be able to improve process and pull those things together. That's where that journey starts to come in of needing leadership support, needing some level of budget to be able to support things. One of the anti-patterns that I do see a lot of is there should be a central team that owns some kind of a tool. But you really should be driving an inner-sourcing model across your organization to support those kinds of things. The last thing you want is a 40-person team running a tool like Backstage. And I've actually seen that in a couple of different places, but it should only be a handful, maybe six. that are managing that central spot, and then having these other teams contribute back to that in one way or another. A lot of the different platforms out there have kind of a plugin model. Say you have a security team or whatever, they can now give you back some kind of code to then implement inside of your portal. And it pushes that towards the edge to the people that understand the thing that they're trying to build
